field_notes.name: Charring a pepper
field_notes.body: The same dry cast-iron pan from July works — but peppers take longer and need to steam afterward. Char them on all sides until the skin is mostly blackened. Drop them into a bowl, cover tight, and leave them for 15 minutes. The skin will slip off cleanly. What's underneath is something the raw pepper never hinted at.

field_notes.name: Figs and time.
field_notes.body: A ripe fig goes from perfect to past-peak in about 24 hours. Buy them the day you plan to eat them, or the day before. If they're already splitting at the base, eat them today. This isn't a problem — it's the season telling you something.

field_notes.name: You don't need to salt eggplant.
field_notes.body: Salting was right for older varieties, which were genuinely bitter. Modern cultivars have had that bred out. What actually matters is high heat. A crowded pan steams; a hot, uncrowded pan chars. Give it room, leave it alone, and it becomes something worth eating.

field_notes.name: Salt it early, rest it after.
field_notes.body: Salt a thick pork chop at least an hour before it cooks — overnight, uncovered in the fridge, is better. The salt pulls moisture out, then draws it back in seasoned, and the surface dries enough to brown. After cooking, let it rest five minutes before cutting. The juices settle back into the meat instead of running onto the board. Two steps that cost nothing and work on every thick cut you'll ever cook.

weekend_meal.name: Thick pork chops, charred nectarines, and pepper sauce.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In August, it's a thick pork chop salted early, seared hard, and rested — with nectarines charred in the same pan.
weekend_meal.card_line: Thick pork chops, nectarines, charred pepper sauce, basil
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: Everything here is on the shopping list. Cook both chops; the second is tomorrow's charred plate or fig toast.
weekend_meal.method: At least an hour ahead — overnight is better — salt the chops well on all sides and leave them uncovered in the fridge. Take them out twenty minutes before cooking and pat them dry. Heat a heavy skillet over medium-high with a thin film of oil until it shimmers. Sear the chops 4 to 5 minutes a side without moving them, then stand them on their fat edge for a minute to render it. They're done when the center is just blushing pink near the bone (140°F if you have a thermometer). Rest them five minutes. While they rest, put the nectarine halves cut side down in the same pan for two or three minutes until they char. Plate the chops with the nectarines, a spoonful of pepper sauce, torn basil, flaky salt, and black pepper.

figs.name: Figs
figs.why_now: Mission figs peak in late July through August. The window is short — often just two or three weeks of genuinely perfect fruit. What you find now was picked ripe and won't be available like this again until next year.
how_to_choose: Deep purple to almost black — that's ripe, not overripe
Slightly soft when gently pressed, especially near the base
Sometimes splitting at the base — that's a good sign
A small bead of sweetness near the stem means it's ready
Avoid pale green or tan figs; they haven't ripened
figs.buy_this_much: 1 pint for the week. Plan to eat most of them within two days of buying.
figs.price_note: Figs are briefly abundant in August and reasonably priced at farmers markets. Grocery store figs are available but often picked underripe for transport — the farmers market version is worth the detour this month.

bell-peppers.name: Bell peppers
bell-peppers.tile_uses: The jar, the sheet pan, the charred plate
bell-peppers.why_now: Red and yellow bell peppers are fully ripened green peppers — and August is when they arrive in abundance. The color change takes weeks on the plant, which is why they cost more and why they taste completely different. The bitterness is gone. What's left is sweet, thick, and worth roasting.
how_to_choose: Fully red or fully yellow — no green patches
Firm and heavy for their size
Glossy skin without soft spots
The thicker the walls, the better for roasting
bell-peppers.buy_this_much: 3–4 peppers for the week. Two go into the house flavor; the rest go into meals.
bell-peppers.price_note: Red and yellow peppers cost more than green because they've spent longer on the plant. In August, supply increases and prices tend to soften slightly.

bell-peppers.one_thing_to_learn: A fully red bell pepper and a green bell pepper are the same vegetable at different points of ripeness. The green one was picked early. This is also why charring works so well on red peppers — there's actual sugar to caramelize.

eggplant.name: Eggplant
eggplant.tile_uses: The sheet pan, the charred plate
eggplant.why_now: Eggplant peaks in late summer — August is when Southern California farms produce them in abundance. The flesh is less bitter than in off-season months, and the skin is thinner. What arrives now roasts into something deeply savory with minimal effort.
how_to_choose: Firm with no soft spots — a soft eggplant will be bitter and seedy
Glossy, taut skin rather than dull or wrinkled
Lighter weight for its size often means fewer seeds
The cap and stem should still look fresh, not dry
eggplant.buy_this_much: 1 large eggplant or 2 small ones for the week.
eggplant.price_note: Eggplant is inexpensive in August when supply peaks. Italian eggplant (the long, narrow variety) and Japanese eggplant roast particularly well.

jalapenos.name: Jalapeños
jalapenos.tile_uses: The hot flavor, the jar, the drink
jalapenos.why_now: Jalapeños are peak summer, and in August the heat and color variation is at its widest. Green jalapeños are grassier; red jalapeños (fully ripened) are fruitier and a little hotter. The house flavor this month uses them alongside peppers — but they earn their place in almost every savory dish on the table.
how_to_choose: Firm and glossy, no soft spots
Green is grassy and mild-to-medium; red is fruity and a bit hotter
Streaks of tan or brown on the skin (corking) indicate more heat — a sign of stress on the plant, which concentrates the capsaicin
Smaller jalapeños tend to be hotter than larger ones
jalapenos.buy_this_much: 3–4 jalapeños. Two go into the house flavor; the rest carry the week.
jalapenos.price_note: Jalapeños are inexpensive year-round but at their best now. Look for them at Mexican grocery stores or the farmers market for the freshest selection.

Firm with no soft spots
Glossy skin, no bruising

nectarines.name: Nectarines
nectarines.why_now: Nectarines are peaches without the fuzz, and in August they often hit their stride when peach season begins to wind down. The flavor is similar — sweet, aromatic, deeply summery — but the skin is thinner and doesn't need peeling. This is the last good stone fruit window before fall.
how_to_choose: Fragrant at the stem end — this is the most reliable test
Gives slightly when gently pressed near the top
Deep color, though variety affects this (yellow and white varieties both have peak moments)
Avoid hard nectarines — they were picked underripe and won't improve meaningfully
nectarines.buy_this_much: 4–5 nectarines for the week. They don't all need to be eaten at once.
nectarines.price_note: Stone fruit is still affordable in August, though supply begins to thin by late in the month. Buy them when you see good ones — the window doesn't come back.

nectarines.one_thing_to_learn: Nectarines and peaches are genetically almost identical — the difference is a single gene that determines whether the skin is fuzzy or smooth. Pink to light red, not gray
A good band of white fat along the edge
